Part A

The isolobal analogy

Fragments that offer the cage the same orbitals and electrons can replace one another.

A
Part A.
Isolobal analogy · fragments

Different fragments, the same three frontier orbitals

Hoffmann (1982): fragments are isolobal when the number, symmetry, approximate energy and shape of their frontier orbitals, and the electrons in them, are similar. Counts: main group v + x − 2; transition metal v + x − 12 (Mingos, 1972; Das, §10.12.11). Orbital drawings schematic.
Each fragment uses three orbitals pointing into the cage (one radial, two tangential for BH). Row one gives 2 skeletal electrons, row two gives 3. ⟷ with the loop is the isolobal symbol. v = valence electrons of the atom, x = electrons from the ligands (H 1, CO 2, Cp 5).

Using the table

Replace each metal fragment by the main-group fragment with the same count, then apply Wade's rules: n + 1 pairs closo, n + 2 nido, n + 3 arachno.

After Mingos, Nature Phys. Sci. 1972, 236, 99, as tabulated in Mingos (2021), Table 2; Das, §10.12.11 (isolobal list).
Metal fragments: v + x − 12 (Fe 8, Co 9, Ni 10, Mn 7; CO 2, Cp 5). Main group: v + x − 2.

BH⁻ ≡ CH: from borane anions to neutral carboranes

BnHn²⁻ → CBn−1Hn⁻ → C2Bn−2Hn

seriesboranedicarbaborane

Das, §10.12.8, Table 10.12.8.1 and figure (reproduced).
Each CH gives 3 skeletal electrons; replacing two BH− by two CH removes the 2− charge but keeps the cage.
Part B

Carboranes

Nomenclature, structures, preparation, reactions and substitution.

B
Part B.
Carboranes · structures

Closo carboranes keep the shape of BnHn²⁻

carboranecage
1,5-C2B3H5trigonal bipyramid
1,6- and 1,2-C2B4H6octahedron
2,4-C2B5H7pentagonal bipyramid
1,2-, 1,7-, 1,12-C2B10H12icosahedron
  • C prefers vertices of low connectivity, and positions far apart.
  • No bridging H; every vertex has one terminal H.
Das, §10.12.8, Fig. 10.12.8.1 (reproduced); Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.1–6.
C is more electronegative than B and contributes one more electron; the most stable isomers keep the carbons apart.
Carboranes · nomenclature

Naming carboranes: five steps

1. Count all cage atoms (B + C): this gives the parent, e.g. 12 → dodecaborane.

2. Add the cage type in italics: closo, nido, arachno.

3. Name the C atoms by replacement prefixes: carba, dicarba (also phospha, thia, cobalta, ferra …).

4. Number the cage and give the C atoms the lowest locants.

5. Add the number of H in parentheses; anions end in -borate with the charge.

Worked example

C2B10H12, C atoms adjacent:
1,2-dicarba-closo-dodecaborane(12)
trivial name: ortho-carborane

Numbering

Start at an apex of lowest connectivity; go round each ring in turn, clockwise, ending at the opposite apex.

Examples and style: Das, §10.12.8 ("1,6-dicarba-closo-hexaborane(6)", "phospha-closo-dodecaborane(12)"); numbering convention as in Hawthorne (1967), Fig. 5.2 and IUPAC boron-cluster recommendations (rule summary given from memory; check against IUPAC Nomenclature of Inorganic Chemistry 2005, IR-6).
Older literature writes the formula with B first (B10C2H12, Das) or C first (C2B10H12); both mean the same cage.

Standard numbering (C1, C2 dark).

Das, §10.12.8 and §10.13.3 (C2B4H6, C2B3H7, PB11H12, 7,8-C2B9H12⁻, 2,3-C2B4H8); CB11H12⁻ name written by the same rules. In PB11H12 no locant is needed: all icosahedral vertices are equivalent.
Nido-C2B9 anions keep the numbering of the icosahedron they came from: removing B3 from 1,2-C2B10H12 and renumbering puts the carbons at 7 and 8 on the open face.
Carboranes · icosahedral isomers

ortho, meta and para-carborane

  • Heating moves the C atoms apart; 1,12 is the most stable.
  • 1,2 ⇌ 1,7 is explained by a diamond–square–diamond path through a cuboctahedron; this path cannot give 1,12.
Das, §10.13.3, Fig. 10.13.3.1 (reproduced); Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.6a (450–500 °C and 500–620 °C).

Carboranes · substitution sites

Where reagents attack ortho-carborane

Why

C is more electronegative than B: the cage is polarised Bδ+–Cδ−. Borons next to carbon are most positive; borons far from carbon are least positive.

Das, §10.13.3 (electrophiles far from C, nucleophiles at B next to C; C–H acidity ortho > meta > para).

Carboranes · substitution at carbon

Substitution at carbon through the dilithio compound

1,2-C2B10H12 + 2 BuLi → 1,2-Li2C2B10H10 + 2 C4H10then CO2, I2, Me2SiCl2, Ph2PCl …
Das, §10.13.3, Scheme 10.13.3.1 (reproduced).
The dilithio compound is a strong nucleophile: CO2 gives the dicarboxylic acid, I2 the diiodide, Ph2PCl the bis(diphenylphosphino) compound, which chelates Fe(CO)3.

Part C

Metallaboranes

Metals bound through B–H–M bridges, or built into the cage.

C
Part C.
Metallaboranes · through hydrogen

Metals bound through M–H–B bridges

  • BH4⁻ binds a metal through one, two or three H (η1, η2, η3). Each M–H–B link is a 3c–2e bond, as in B2H6.
  • Zr(BH4)4: volatile, molecular; Zr is 12-coordinate by H.
  • (CO)4Mn(B3H8): Mn(CO)4 replaces a BH2 unit; counts as arachno, like B4H10.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.7A, p. 312; Das, §10.12.11; Zr(BH4)4: Greenwood & Earnshaw, 2nd edn, §6.3.3.
The drawings show the three coordination modes schematically.
Metallaboranes · metal in the cage

Fe(CO)3 and CpCo in place of BH

B5H9
drag to rotate

B4H8Fe(CO)3: 4 × 2 + 4 + 2 = 14 e = 7 pairs, n = 5 → nido, like B5H9. CpCo gives apical (1-) and basal (2-) isomers.

Das, §10.12.11, Fig. 10.12.11.1 (reproduced); Mingos (2021), §9.2. 3D model built from B5H9 for teaching.
Preparation: B5H9 with Fe(CO)5 replaces the apical BH by Fe(CO)3, losing CO (Das).

Part D

Metallacarboranes

The dicarbollide ion as an inorganic cyclopentadienide.

D
Part D.
Metallacarboranes · the ligand

The dicarbollide ion, [7,8-C2B9H11]²⁻

  • Open pentagonal C2B3 face: five orbitals, six electrons, as in C5H5⁻.
  • Binds a metal η5 as a 6-electron, 2− ligand; the metal fills the missing 12th vertex.
  • Name: Spanish olla, a pot.

Isolobal

C2B9H11²⁻ ≡ C5H5⁻; its orbitals point towards the vacant vertex, so they overlap well with a metal there.

Das, §10.13.3, Fig. 10.13.3.2 (reproduced; labels (c) and (d) described from the drawings); Hawthorne (1967), §5.6B.7, Fig. 5.32.
Preparation from ortho-carborane is on the reactions-at-boron slide: EtO− removes B3, NaH removes the bridging proton.
Metallacarboranes · sandwiches

The carborane analogue of ferrocene

2 C2B9H11²⁻ + FeCl2 → [Fe(η5-C2B9H11)2]²⁻ + 2 Cl⁻
[FeII(C2B9H11)2]²⁻ ⇌ [FeIII(C2B9H11)2]⁻ + e⁻
C2B9H11²⁻ + C5H5⁻ + Fe²⁺ → [CpFe(C2B9H11)]⁻
C2B9H11²⁻ + BrRe(CO)5 → [(C2B9H11)Re(CO)3]⁻ + Br⁻ + 2 CO

Fe(II) d⁶ + 2 × 6 = 18 electrons, as in ferrocene. Co(III), Ni(III/IV), Cr(III) give similar sandwiches.

[Fe(C2B9H11)2]²⁻

Das, §10.13.3; M. F. Hawthorne, D. C. Young, P. A. Wegner, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1965, 87, 1818; Hawthorne (1967), §5.7B. Models idealised.

Metallacarboranes · counting

Two ways to count a metallacarborane

As a metal complex

  • Each dicarbollide: 6 e, 2−.
  • [Fe(C2B9H11)2]²⁻: Fe²⁺ d⁶ + 12 = 18 e.
  • [Co(C2B9H11)2]⁻: Co³⁺ d⁶ + 12 = 18 e.

As a cluster

  • [(C2B9H11)Re(CO)3]⁻: Re(CO)3 7 + 6 − 12 = 1; + 6 (2 CH) + 18 (9 BH) + 1 (charge) = 26 e = 13 pairs, n = 12 → closo.

Both counts agree: 18 electrons at the metal and n + 1 pairs in the cage both mean "all bonding orbitals filled".

Das, §10.12.10 and §10.13.3; Mingos (2021), pp. 20–22.
Hawthorne's group merged the 18-electron rule with the 2n + 2 skeletal electron requirement.
Metallacarboranes · beyond twelve vertices

Polyhedral expansion: reduce, then add a metal

  • Two electrons open closo-C2B10H12 to a nido dianion (n + 2 pairs).
  • A metal fragment caps the open face: the cage closes again with 13 vertices, e.g. CpCo(C2B10H12).
Method of G. B. Dunks, M. M. McKown, M. F. Hawthorne, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1971, 93, 2541 (reference from memory); counting as in Das, §10.12.8.
Wade's rules used as a synthetic plan.
Applications

What carboranes and metallacarboranes are used for

Nuclear waste

Chlorinated cobalt bis(dicarbollide) extracts 137Cs and 90Sr from acidic waste (UNEX process).

Weakly coordinating anions

CB11H12⁻ and [Co(C2B9H11)2]⁻ stabilise very reactive cations; H(CHB11Cl11) is a carborane superacid.

Polymers

m-Carborane–siloxane polymers resist heat and oxidation.

Medicine

Boron-rich cages for neutron capture therapy; carboranyl as a 3D substitute for phenyl in drug design.

R. S. Herbst et al., Sep. Sci. Technol. 2003, 38, 2685; M. Juhasz et al., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2004, 43, 5352; carborane–siloxane polymers: Das, §10.13.3.
All uses come from the stability of the cage and the spreading of charge over a large surface.
Summary

Key points

  • Isolobal fragments (BH ≡ Fe(CO)3 ≡ CpCo; CH ≡ BH⁻ ≡ Co(CO)3) can replace one another in a cage without changing its type.
  • Carboranes are named as dicarba-closo/nido-boranes, with lowest locants to C: 1,2-dicarba-closo-dodecaborane(12).
  • Made from boranes and alkynes; 1,2 → 1,7 → 1,12 on heating.
  • C–H: lithiation; B far from C: electrophiles; B next to C: nucleophiles, giving dicarbollide.
  • Dicarbollide ≡ Cp⁻: sandwich and half-sandwich metallacarboranes obeying both 18-electron and Wade counts.
Das, §10.12–10.13; Hawthorne (1967), ch. 5; Mingos (2021).
Ask students to name nido-7,9-C2B9H12−.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Name C2B10H12 with the C atoms opposite each other.
1,12-dicarba-closo-dodecaborane(12), para-carborane.
2. Show that Co(CO)3 is isolobal with CH.
9 + 6 − 12 = 3 skeletal electrons in three orbitals; C–H: 4 + 1 − 2 = 3.
3. Which boron of ortho-carborane does EtO⁻ remove, and why?
B3 (or B6), bonded to both C: the most positive boron.
4. Count B4H8Fe(CO)3.
8 + 4 + 2 = 14 e = 7 pairs, n = 5: nido square pyramid.
Based on these notes.
